lessons.title: Methods and Lambdas
lessons.explanation:
# 02 · Methods and Lambdas

Every beginner CLI project starts as one long `main` and gets better the
day it is split into methods that take arguments and return answers. This
module is about that split, and about the move after it: passing
*behaviour* around — a rule, a formatter, a retry policy — as a value.

Java got lambdas late (Java 8) and bolted them onto interfaces. Once you
see that a lambda is "an object implementing a one-method interface", the
whole `java.util.function` package stops being a zoo.

## The mental model

### 1 · A lambda is an instance of a functional interface

```java
Predicate<String> notBlank = s -> !s.isBlank();     // test(String) -> boolean
Function<String, Integer> len = String::length;     // apply(String) -> Integer
Supplier<LocalDate> today = () -> LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1);  // get()
```

There is no "function type". The *target type* — the variable, parameter
or return type — decides which interface the lambda implements.

| interface | method | shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Function<A, B>` | `apply` | A → B |
| `UnaryOperator<T>` | `apply` | T → T |
| `BiFunction<A, B, C>` | `apply` | (A, B) → C |
| `Predicate<T>` | `test` | T → boolean |
| `Supplier<T>` | `get` | () → T |
| `Consumer<T>` | `accept` | T → void |
| `IntUnaryOperator`, `IntSupplier`, … | | primitive versions, no boxing |

### 2 · Lambdas capture values, and only effectively-final ones

```java
int limit = 3;
Predicate<String> shortEnough = s -> s.length() <= limit;  // fine
limit = 4;   // now the lambda above no longer compiles
```

To keep *mutable* state in a closure, capture a final reference to
something mutable — an `int[1]`, an `AtomicInteger`, a field.

### 3 · Functions that build functions

```java
static Predicate<String> maxLength(int n) { return s -> s.length() <= n; }
var rule = maxLength(10).and(s -> s.endsWith("?"));
```

`and`, `or`, `negate`, `andThen`, `compose`, `Comparator.comparing(...)`
— the JDK's own higher-order functions. Learn their order rules once.

### 4 · Method references are lambdas with a name

`Integer::parseInt` (static), `String::length` (unbound — the first
argument is the receiver), `System.out::println` (bound), `Book::new`
(constructor).

## The details that bite

1. **`f.andThen(g)` runs f first; `f.compose(g)` runs g first.**
2. **A `for (int i…)` variable can't be captured** — copy it into a local
   inside the loop body. (This is the compiler preventing the classic
   "every callback sees the last i" bug.)
3. **`stream().count()` returns `long`.** Cast or use `Math.toIntExact`.
4. **`List.of(...)` is immutable.** `sort`, `add`, `remove` on it throw
   `UnsupportedOperationException`. Sort a copy.
5. **`computeIfAbsent` never stores `null`** — a null result is
   recomputed every time.
6. **`Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is negative.** Two's complement has one
   more negative number than positive.
7. **Overload resolution happens at compile time** and prefers widening,
   then boxing, then varargs.
8. **No tail calls.** Deep recursion overflows the stack; recurse on
   structure, loop on size.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-varargs-and-overloads.java` | ★☆☆ | sum of anything, and "at least one" tags |
| 02 | `02-functional-interfaces.java` | ★☆☆ | applyTwice, countMatching, pipe |
| 03 | `03-closures-and-capture.java` | ★★☆ | independent counters, and lambdas in a loop |
| 04 | `04-method-references.java` | ★☆☆ | the four kinds of `::` in a library import |
| 05 | `05-predicate-rules.java` | ★★☆ | named validation rules, combined and reported |
| 06 | `06-recursion.java` | ★★☆ | digit sums (and the abs trap), flattening nested lists |
| 07 | `07-memoize.java` | ★★★ | a cache wrapper that remembers null too |
| 08 | `08-retry.java` | ★★★ | retry with suppressed exceptions |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows.

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/03-collections-and-streams`

javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/01-v.instructions:
**Concepts:** varargs · overloading · static methods · StringBuilder  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A to-do manager lets you sum estimates and print hashtags. Write sum,
which takes any number of ints (none at all → 0), and tags, which takes
at least one tag and then any number more, and renders them as
"#a #b #c" — tags are trimmed, and blank ones are skipped.

    sum()                         → 0
    sum(1, 2, 3)                  → 6
    sum(new int[] {5, 5})         → 10
    tags("java")                  → "#java"
    tags("java", " cli ", " ")    → "#java #cli"

hint: inside the method, int... values is just an int[].
javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/01-v.explanation:
`int... values` is syntax sugar for an int[] parameter: the CALLER may
list values, pass nothing (an empty array, never null), or hand over an
existing array — all three end up as the same int[] inside. So sum is
an ordinary loop over an array.
tags shows the idiom for "at least one": a normal parameter first, then
the varargs. `tags()` with no arguments simply does not compile, which
beats a runtime check. Only the LAST parameter may be varargs.
Building output in a loop wants a StringBuilder (or a StringJoiner /
String.join over a filtered list), not `s += ...`, which copies the
whole string each time. Here the blank-tag rule makes the separator
fiddly with a raw StringBuilder; StringJoiner(" ") puts separators only
BETWEEN the parts it actually receives.
Overloading note: Java picks an overload at COMPILE time and prefers
widening, then boxing, then varargs — so a varargs overload is the last
resort, and adding a sum(int, int) later would silently take over every
two-argument call.

javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/02-f.instructions:
**Concepts:** lambdas · Function · UnaryOperator · Predicate · generics  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Three tiny utilities every later exercise leans on. applyTwice runs a
function on a value, then on the result. countMatching counts the items
a predicate accepts. pipe glues two functions into one: first, then
second.

    applyTwice(x -> x * 3, 2)                        → 18
    countMatching(List.of(1, 5, 10), n -> n > 3)     → 2
    pipe(String::trim, String::length).apply(" ab ") → 2
    pipe(x -> x + 1, x -> x * 2).apply(3)            → 8

hint: a Function's method is apply; a Predicate's is test.
javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/02-f.explanation:
Java has no function TYPES — it has functional INTERFACES: any interface
with exactly one abstract method. A lambda or method reference is an
instance of whichever one the context asks for. java.util.function
gives you the standard shapes: Function<A, B> (apply), UnaryOperator<T>
(a Function<T, T>), Predicate<T> (test, returns boolean), Supplier<T>
(get), Consumer<T> (accept), plus primitive versions like IntPredicate
that avoid boxing.
applyTwice is f.apply(f.apply(value)). countMatching is a loop with a
test, or items.stream().filter(test).count() — note count() returns a
long, so the int return type needs a cast (or Math.toIntExact).
pipe returns a NEW function: a lambda that closes over first and
second. The JDK already has it — first.andThen(second) — and the order
trap is exactly the 4th example: andThen runs first-then-second;
compose runs the ARGUMENT first. 3 + 1 then * 2 is 8; the other order
gives 7.

javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/03-c.instructions:
**Concepts:** closures · effectively final · IntSupplier · capture in loops  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A quiz engine numbers its questions with a counter object, and builds a
row of "add k" functions for bonus points. Write counter: each call to
the returned supplier gives the next number, starting at start; two
counters never share a count. Then write adders: adders(n) is a list of
n functions where the k-th one adds k.

    var next = counter(1);
    next.getAsInt(), next.getAsInt(), next.getAsInt()   → 1, 2, 3
    adders(3).get(2).applyAsInt(10)                     → 12

hint: a lambda may only capture locals that are never reassigned.
javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/03-c.explanation:
A lambda captures local variables BY VALUE, and Java only lets it
capture ones that are effectively final — never reassigned after
initialisation. So `int n = start; return () -> n++;` does not compile.
That rule is deliberate: it rules out the data races and the "which
value did I capture?" confusion other languages allow.
To keep mutable state you capture a final reference to something
mutable: a one-element array (`int[] n = {start}` then `n[0]++`), an
AtomicInteger (`n.getAndIncrement()`), or a small class with a field.
Each call to counter(...) creates a NEW box, so two counters are
independent — the state lives per closure, not per method.
In adders the loop variable `k` of a classic for loop IS reassigned (by
k++), so `x -> x + k` does not compile. Copy it first: `int add = k;`
— a fresh effectively-final local each iteration. C# and JavaScript
programmers know the bug this prevents: every lambda seeing the final
value of the loop variable. Java turns it into a compile error.

javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/04-m.instructions:
**Concepts:** method references · Comparator · constructor refs · streams  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A library tracker imports raw text. Write parseAll (strings to ints; a
bad number throws NumberFormatException), byLength (shortest first,
alphabetical among equal lengths, the input list left untouched) and
toBooks (one Book per title). The record Book is defined above the code
you edit. Use method references where they fit.

    parseAll(List.of("1", "22"))                  → [1, 22]
    byLength(List.of("ccc", "bb", "a", "aa"))     → [a, aa, bb, ccc]
    toBooks(List.of("Dune"))                      → [Book[title=Dune]]

hint: List.of(...) is immutable — sorting it in place throws.
javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/04-m.explanation:
A method reference is a lambda whose body is one call, written by name.
There are four shapes: static (Integer::parseInt, x -> parseInt(x)),
bound instance (System.out::println, x -> out.println(x)), unbound
instance (String::length, s -> s.length() — the first argument becomes
the receiver), and constructor (Book::new, t -> new Book(t)).
parseAll is map(Integer::parseInt).toList(). Stream.toList() (Java 16+)
returns an unmodifiable list, which is what you want to hand back.
byLength needs a two-level ordering: Comparator.comparingInt(String::
length).thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()). Sorting must happen
on a COPY — `words.sort(...)` on a List.of throws
UnsupportedOperationException, and on a mutable list it silently
reorders the caller's data. stream().sorted(...) copies for you.
comparingInt (not comparing) avoids boxing every length into Integer.
toBooks is map(Book::new): the compiler sees a Function<String, Book>
is wanted and finds the one-argument constructor.

javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/05-p.instructions:
**Concepts:** Predicate · and/negate · higher-order functions · LinkedHashMap  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A quiz engine validates new question text with small named rules.
Write notBlank (null or whitespace-only fails), maxLength(n), allOf
(passes when every rule passes; no rules at all → passes) and failures,
which returns the NAMES of the rules a value breaks, in the map's order.

    notBlank().test("  ")                         → false
    maxLength(3).test("abcd")                     → false
    allOf(List.of(notBlank(), maxLength(5)))
        .test("hello")                            → true
    failures("", {"required"=notBlank(), "short"=maxLength(3)})
                                                  → ["required"]

hint: Predicate already has and(...), and an empty "and" is true.
javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/05-p.explanation:
A rule is just a Predicate<String>, so rules can be stored in lists and
maps, passed around and combined — validation becomes data instead of
a staircase of ifs.
notBlank must handle null BEFORE calling isBlank, or the rule itself
throws on the very input it exists to reject. maxLength(n) returns a
lambda that captures n: a function that builds functions.
allOf folds the list with Predicate::and, starting from the identity
for "and", which is a predicate that always says true:
rules.stream().reduce(x -> true, Predicate::and). That starting value
is why "no rules" passes — the same reason an empty sum is 0.
failures walks the map's entries and keeps the keys whose rule fails.
The order guarantee comes from the MAP, not from you: a HashMap would
return names in hash order. The tests pass a LinkedHashMap (insertion
order); TreeMap would sort by name. Pick the map that states the order
you promise.

javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/06-r.instructions:
**Concepts:** recursion · base case · instanceof patterns · Math.abs trap  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Two recursive helpers. sumDigits adds up the decimal digits of a long
(the sign is ignored). flatten turns arbitrarily nested lists into one
flat list, in reading order; empty inner lists simply vanish.

    sumDigits(1234)                                → 10
    sumDigits(-56)                                 → 11
    sumDigits(Long.MIN_VALUE)                      → 89
    flatten(List.of(1, List.of(2, List.of(3)), 4)) → [1, 2, 3, 4]

hint: Math.abs(Long.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.
javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/06-r.explanation:
Every recursion is a base case plus a step that makes the problem
smaller. For sumDigits the base case is 0 (no digits left) and the step
peels off the last digit: |n % 10| + sumDigits(n / 10). Division moves
toward zero, so negative numbers terminate too.
The trap is the "obvious" first move, n = Math.abs(n). Two's complement
has one more negative number than positive ones, so Math.abs(Long.
MIN_VALUE) overflows back to Long.MIN_VALUE — still negative — and the
digit loop produces nonsense. Taking the absolute value of each
REMAINDER (always between -9 and 9) side-steps the edge entirely.
(Math.absExact would at least throw instead of lying.)
flatten recurses on structure rather than numbers: for each element,
if it is itself a List, flatten it and add everything; otherwise add
the element. `if (item instanceof List<?> inner)` is the Java 16+
pattern form — test and cast in one step, no (List<?>) cast. Passing an
accumulator list down (instead of allocating and concatenating at each
level) keeps it linear.
Java has no tail-call optimisation: recursion depth is bounded by the
stack (a few thousand frames). Fine for digits and nesting; use a loop
for anything that grows with the input size.

javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/07-m.instructions:
**Concepts:** higher-order functions · HashMap cache · null values · closures  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

An order system looks up shipping quotes through a slow function. Write
memoize: it takes a function and returns a new one that gives the same
answers but calls the original at most once per distinct input. A null
answer counts as an answer — it is remembered too. Two memoized
functions never share a cache.

    var quote = memoize(slowQuote);    // slowQuote counts its calls
    quote.apply("10115");
    quote.apply("10115");              → slowQuote ran once

hint: Map.computeIfAbsent does not store null results.
javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/07-m.explanation:
memoize is a function that returns a function, and the returned lambda
closes over a cache that memoize created. Each call to memoize builds a
new HashMap, which is exactly why two memoized functions are
independent — the cache's lifetime is the closure's.
The tempting one-liner is `return k -> cache.computeIfAbsent(k, f);`.
It is right for most inputs and wrong for this spec: computeIfAbsent
treats a null result as "no mapping" and calls f again next time. A
lookup that legitimately answers "nothing" (no quote for that zip)
would hit the slow service on every call.
The fix separates "absent" from "present with value null":
containsKey first, then get — or store Optional values. That
distinction (missing key vs null value) is a recurring Java theme;
Map.get alone cannot tell them apart.
Two more real-world caveats: this cache never evicts, so it grows
forever (fine for a bounded key space), and a HashMap is not
thread-safe — a shared memoizer needs ConcurrentHashMap, which in turn
refuses null values outright. Also never call computeIfAbsent
recursively on the same HashMap; since Java 9 it throws
ConcurrentModificationException.

javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/08-r.instructions:
**Concepts:** Supplier · exceptions as values · suppressed exceptions · loops  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

A bank simulator talks to a flaky ledger service. Write retry: call the
action up to `attempts` times and return the first successful result.
If every attempt throws, rethrow the LAST RuntimeException, with each
earlier failure attached DIRECTLY to it as a suppressed exception,
oldest first. attempts below 1 is a programming error:
IllegalArgumentException.

    retry(3, () -> "ok")                    → "ok" (one call)
    retry(3, failsTwiceThenReturns(42))     → 42   (three calls)
    retry(3, alwaysFails)                   → throws the 3rd failure;
                                  its suppressed: [1st failure, 2nd]

hint: Throwable has addSuppressed(...) and getSuppressed().
javabootcamp/02-methods-and-lambdas/08-r.explanation:
A Supplier<T> is "a computation you can run later", which is what makes
retry possible at all: the caller hands over the WORK, not its result.
The loop collects every failure in a list. After the loop, the last
one is what the caller sees — usually the most relevant — and every
earlier one is attached to it with addSuppressed, oldest first. The
tempting shortcut, e.addSuppressed(previous) inside the catch, builds
a CHAIN instead (3rd holds 2nd, 2nd holds 1st): nothing is lost, but
getSuppressed() on the thrown exception shows only one of them.
Why not just log and drop the earlier ones? Because the first failure
is often the real cause (a timeout) and later ones are noise (a
connection pool now exhausted). Suppressed exceptions show up in the
stack trace under "Suppressed:", so nothing is lost.
Validate attempts BEFORE the loop: with attempts = 0 the loop never
runs, the list is empty, and failures.get(-1) crashes with a confusing
IndexOutOfBoundsException. Fail fast with IllegalArgumentException.
Real retry adds a delay between attempts (with backoff) and only
retries errors that are worth retrying — never a validation error.
Here there is no sleep, so the tests stay fast and deterministic.
